title: Thermodynamics: Energy, Enthalpy, and Entropy
description: Laws of thermodynamics and the spontaneity of chemical reactions

concepts.title: The Laws of Thermodynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Thermodynamics governs energy flow in chemical systems. The four laws:

Zeroth law: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — this defines temperature.
First law: energy is conserved: ΔU = q + w (internal energy change = heat absorbed + work done on system).
Second law: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases; for spontaneous processes, ΔS_universe > 0.
Third law: the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero — this anchors the absolute entropy scale.

The first and second laws together determine whether a reaction is spontaneous and how much work can be extracted from it.

concepts.title: Enthalpy and Hess's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Enthalpy (H) is defined as H = U + PV. At constant pressure (most lab reactions): ΔH = q_p. Exothermic reactions have ΔH < 0; endothermic have ΔH > 0.

Hess's Law: enthalpy is a state function — ΔH for a reaction is the same regardless of the path taken. This allows indirect calculation of ΔH using standard enthalpies of formation (ΔH°_f):

ΔH°_rxn = Σ ΔH°_f (products) − Σ ΔH°_f (reactants)

Standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of compound forms from its elements in their standard states. For elements in standard states, ΔH°_f = 0 by definition.

concepts.title: Entropy and Gibbs Free Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
Entropy (S) measures dispersal of energy or disorder. Processes that increase molecular freedom — gas expansion, mixing, melting — increase entropy.

Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy into the ultimate spontaneity criterion at constant T and P:

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

A reaction is spontaneous if ΔG < 0. ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. The sign of ΔG depends on both ΔH and ΔS — and their interplay at a given temperature. For example, an endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0) can still be spontaneous at high T if ΔS > 0 (entropy-driven). Ice melting at room temperature is a classic case: ΔH > 0 but TΔS overwhelms it.

title: Chemical Kinetics
description: Rate laws, activation energy, and reaction mechanisms

concepts.title: Rate Laws and Rate Constants
concepts.contentHtml:
The rate of a reaction is the rate of change of concentration over time. For A + B → products, the rate law is:

rate = k[A]^m[B]^n

where k is the rate constant, and m, n are the orders with respect to each reactant. The overall order is m + n. Crucially, orders must be determined experimentally — they cannot be read from the balanced equation (only for elementary steps).

Units of k depend on overall order: first order (s⁻¹); second order (L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹).

For a first-order reaction: [A] = [A]₀ e^(−kt). The half-life t₁/₂ = ln2/k is constant — independent of concentration. This is the basis of radioactive decay and some drug elimination kinetics.

concepts.title: Activation Energy and the Arrhenius Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
The Arrhenius equation describes how rate constant depends on temperature:

k = A e^(−Ea/RT)

where A is the pre-exponential factor (collision frequency × steric factor), Ea is the activation energy (minimum energy to reach the transition state), R is the gas constant, and T is temperature in kelvin.

Taking the logarithm: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. Plotting ln k vs 1/T gives a straight line with slope −Ea/R — the standard way to measure Ea experimentally.

The rule of thumb 'reaction rate doubles for every 10°C rise' follows from Arrhenius with a typical Ea ~50 kJ/mol. This has huge practical implications: enzymes work at 37°C; autoclaving at 121°C kills bacteria (millions-fold rate increase for protein denaturation).

concepts.title: Reaction Mechanisms and the Rate-Determining Step
concepts.contentHtml:
A balanced chemical equation does not reveal the mechanism. Most reactions occur via a sequence of elementary steps. The rate-determining step (RDS) is the slowest step — it controls the overall rate, like the bottleneck in a pipeline.

For a mechanism A ⇌ B (fast equilibrium) then B → C (slow, RDS):
rate = k₂[B] = k₂·K[A] → rate ∝ [A]

The steady-state approximation: the concentration of intermediates is assumed constant (rate of formation = rate of consumption). This is the foundation for the Michaelis–Menten rate equation in enzymology.

Distinguishing between proposed mechanisms requires kinetic experiments (varying concentrations), isotope labelling (tracking which bonds break), and spectroscopic detection of intermediates.

title: Chemical Equilibrium
description: Equilibrium constants, Le Chatelier's principle, and Kp vs Kc

concepts.title: The Equilibrium Constant
concepts.contentHtml:
For the reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, at equilibrium:

K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b

K_c is dimensionless (formally, concentrations divided by the standard concentration 1 M) and depends only on temperature. Pure solids and liquids are excluded (their activities = 1).

The reaction quotient Q has the same form but uses non-equilibrium concentrations. If Q < K: reaction proceeds forward. If Q > K: reaction proceeds backward. If Q = K: system is at equilibrium.

For gas-phase reactions, K_p uses partial pressures instead of concentrations: K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn, where Δn = (total moles of gaseous products) − (total moles of gaseous reactants).

concepts.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to partially counteract the disturbance and reach a new equilibrium.

Consequences for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol):
— Add N₂ or H₂: shifts right (more NH₃)
— Increase pressure: shifts toward fewer moles of gas → right (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas)
— Increase temperature: shifts toward the endothermic direction → left (less NH₃ at higher T)
— Add catalyst: no effect on position — only on how fast equilibrium is reached

Le Chatelier does not change K — only temperature changes K. Everything else changes Q, which then relaxes to the same K.

concepts.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Equilibrium
concepts.contentHtml:
The equilibrium constant K and Gibbs free energy are related by:

ΔG° = −RT ln K

This is one of the most important equations in chemistry. A large K (products favoured) → ΔG° strongly negative. K = 1 → ΔG° = 0. K < 1 → ΔG° positive (reactants favoured).

At non-standard conditions: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. When Q = K, ΔG = 0 — equilibrium. Reactions proceed in the direction that decreases ΔG (i.e., increases Q toward K if Q < K, or decreases Q toward K if Q > K).

This connects thermodynamics and kinetics: ΔG° tells you the equilibrium position, not the rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically favourable (ΔG° << 0) but kinetically slow (high Ea).

title: Quantum Chemistry and Spectroscopy
description: Wave-particle duality, atomic orbitals, and how light probes molecular structure

concepts.title: Wave-Particle Duality and the Schrödinger Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
In quantum mechanics, particles exhibit wave-like behaviour. De Broglie showed that any particle with momentum p has an associated wavelength: λ = h/p.

The Schrödinger equation gives the wavefunction Ψ, whose square |Ψ|² gives the probability density for finding the particle at a given location. For the hydrogen atom, exact solutions yield the familiar atomic orbitals: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3d, etc.

Each orbital is characterised by three quantum numbers:
— n (principal): energy and size
— l (azimuthal): shape (0=s, 1=p, 2=d, 3=f)
— m_l (magnetic): orientation

The Heisenberg uncertainty principle: Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2. You cannot know both position and momentum precisely — this is fundamental, not a measurement limitation.

concepts.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Molecular orbital (MO) theory builds molecular wavefunctions as linear combinations of atomic orbitals (LCAO). When two atomic orbitals combine, they give two MOs: a bonding MO (lower energy, electron density between nuclei) and an antibonding MO* (higher energy, node between nuclei).

The bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) / 2. Bond order > 0: stable molecule. Bond order 0: molecule does not form. O₂ by MO theory has two electrons in degenerate π* orbitals — one each (Hund's rule) — predicting O₂ is paramagnetic. This was a triumph of MO theory over Lewis structures.

MO theory also explains why He₂ does not form (bond order = 0) and why H₂⁺ exists (bond order = 0.5).

concepts.title: Spectroscopy: IR, UV/Vis, and NMR
concepts.contentHtml:
Spectroscopy uses light–matter interaction to determine molecular structure and composition.

Infrared (IR) spectroscopy: molecules absorb IR radiation at frequencies matching their vibrational modes. Each functional group has characteristic stretching frequencies: O–H ~3200–3600 cm⁻¹; C=O ~1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C≡N ~2200 cm⁻¹. IR identifies functional groups.

UV/Vis spectroscopy: electronic transitions; chromophores with π electrons absorb in the UV/Vis range (Beer–Lambert law: A = εcl). Used to quantify concentration and study conjugated systems.

NMR spectroscopy: nuclear spin transitions in a magnetic field. Chemical shift, integration, and splitting patterns identify connectivity (covered in Organic Chemistry). ¹³C NMR and 2D NMR (COSY, NOESY) extend structural information.

title: Electrochemistry
description: Galvanic cells, standard electrode potentials, and electrolysis

concepts.title: Electrochemical Cells
concepts.contentHtml:
An electrochemical cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy (galvanic cell) or vice versa (electrolytic cell). The Daniell cell is classic: Zn anode | ZnSO₄(aq) || CuSO₄(aq) | Cu cathode.

At the anode (oxidation): Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
At the cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

The cell potential: E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode. For Daniell: +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. E°_cell > 0 means the reaction is spontaneous. The salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ion flow without mixing the solutions.

concepts.title: The Nernst Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
Under non-standard conditions (concentrations ≠ 1 M, temperature ≠ 25°C), the cell potential is given by the Nernst equation:

E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q

At 25°C, using log base 10: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q

where n = number of electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol), Q = reaction quotient.

Applications:
— pH meters exploit the Nernst equation: the H⁺ activity determines the glass electrode potential
— Concentration cells have no net chemical reaction (same half-cells) but different concentrations → non-zero EMF
— The relationship ΔG = −nFE links thermodynamics and electrochemistry

concepts.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
Electrolysis uses an external voltage to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. Applications: electroplating (Cu, Ni, Ag onto metals), Hall–Héroult process (aluminium from Al₂O₃), chlor-alkali process (Cl₂ and NaOH from NaCl(aq)).

Faraday's laws of electrolysis:
1. Mass of substance deposited is proportional to charge passed: m = (M/nF) × Q = (M/nF) × It
2. Equal charges deposit equivalent amounts of different substances (equimolar electrons).

These laws are used to calculate how much product is produced from a given current and time. Electrochemistry also underpins lithium-ion batteries (LiCoO₂ cathode / graphite anode), fuel cells (H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, generating electricity), and corrosion (an unintended galvanic cell).

title: Statistical Thermodynamics
description: Bridging molecular states to macroscopic thermodynamics

concepts.title: Boltzmann's Bridge
concepts.contentHtml:
Boltzmann's S = k_B ln Ω links thermodynamic entropy to the number of microstates. Statistical thermodynamics derives macroscopic quantities — internal energy, free energy, entropy, heat capacity — from molecular partition functions.

For a system in thermal equilibrium, the probability of a microstate of energy E is e^(-E/k_B T) / Z, where Z is the partition function: Z = Σ e^(-E_i/k_B T).

From Z you derive everything. ⟨E⟩ = -∂ln Z/∂β; F = -k_B T ln Z; S = -∂F/∂T. The whole macroscopic edifice falls out of the partition function.

concepts.title: Equipartition & Heat Capacities
concepts.contentHtml:
For classical degrees of freedom, equipartition gives ½ k_B T per quadratic mode. A monoatomic gas has 3 translational modes, hence c_V = 3R/2.

Diatomic molecules add 2 rotational modes (room temp) → c_V = 5R/2. Vibrational modes only contribute at high T because their quanta ℏω are comparable to or larger than k_B T.

The freezing-out of vibrational modes at low T (Einstein, Debye) was an early hint of quantization — equipartition fails when quantum gaps matter.

concepts.title: From States to Free Energies
concepts.contentHtml:
Equilibrium constants come from differences in molecular partition functions. Reaction free energy: ΔG° = -RT ln K, with K calculated from the partition functions of products and reactants.

This is how computational chemistry predicts equilibria — not by looking up data but by computing molecular partition functions from quantum chemistry.

Modern free-energy methods extend this to solution and biomolecular systems, where direct partition function evaluation isn't possible.

concepts.title: The Photoexcited State
concepts.contentHtml:
Absorbing a photon promotes a molecule to an electronic excited state. Excited states have different reactivity than ground states — different orbital occupations, different geometries, often different selectivities.

Photochemistry is driven by these excited-state reactivities. Same molecule, different chemistry, depending on whether you give it heat (ground-state pathway) or light (excited-state pathway).

concepts.title: Jablonski Diagrams
concepts.contentHtml:
A Jablonski diagram shows the manifold of electronic and vibrational states for a molecule. Absorption (S₀ → S₁), internal conversion, intersystem crossing (S₁ → T₁), fluorescence (S₁ → S₀ + photon), phosphorescence (T₁ → S₀ + photon).

Each pathway has characteristic timescales: vibrational relaxation ~ps; fluorescence ~ns; phosphorescence ~µs to seconds.

The diagram organizes all photophysics — and predicts which pathway dominates for any given molecule and condition.

concepts.title: Modern Photochemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
Visible-light photoredox catalysis (Ru, Ir polypyridyls; organic dyes) drives radical chemistry under mild conditions. Macmillan and others have developed many synthetic photoredox methods over the past 15 years.

Photodynamic therapy uses light-activated drugs to kill tumors. Solar fuels research aims to use sunlight directly to split water and reduce CO₂. Optogenetics activates specific neurons with light, transforming neuroscience.

Photochemistry has gone from curiosity to practical tool — and from fluorescence physics to solar-energy conversion.

title: Surface & Colloid Physical Chemistry
description: Where bulk thermodynamics meets the interface

concepts.title: Surface Tension
concepts.contentHtml:
At a liquid surface, molecules have fewer neighbors and are pulled inward — creating surface tension γ. Water's γ ≈ 72 mN/m (high, due to hydrogen bonding); ethanol ≈ 22 (low, mostly van der Waals).

Soap molecules (surfactants) reduce surface tension by adsorbing at interfaces with their hydrophilic heads in water and tails in air or oil. That's how detergents work.

concepts.title: Colloids and Suspensions
concepts.contentHtml:
A colloid is a suspension of particles ~1 nm to 1 µm — large enough to scatter light (Tyndall effect) but small enough to stay dispersed.

Milk (fat in water), mayonnaise (oil-in-water emulsion), fog (water in air), gels — all are colloids. Stability comes from electrostatic repulsion (zeta potential) or steric protection (polymer coats).

Disrupt the stabilization (add salt, heat, change pH) and the colloid coagulates. Cheese-making is a controlled coagulation of casein micelles in milk.

concepts.title: Capillarity & Wetting
concepts.contentHtml:
Capillarity: liquids rise (or fall) in narrow tubes due to balance of surface tension and gravity. The Jurin's law: h = 2γ cos θ / (ρ g r). Water rises in glass capillaries; mercury depresses.

Capillarity helps sap rise in trees (though transpiration pull does most of the work), ink moving along a fiber, wicking in fabrics, and surface-tension micropumps.

Wetting (covered earlier): contact angle balances γ_sl, γ_sv, γ_lv. Bringing all three concepts together — surface tension, colloids, capillarity — physical chemistry of interfaces shapes everyday phenomena.
